name: Rafael Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I work for Marlow Fit-Out, a contractor doing restaurants, gyms and shop refits around town. It's fast work: strip out the old place, put in new lighting, kitchen supplies and data points, and hand it back before the opening night. Weekends I do my own small jobs, and I use AI every day for those, pricing, reading spec sheets, writing up certificates. I love a finished restaurant with all the lights on for the first time. What wears me out is being on site till midnight because the owner changed the layout again.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Sofia, my partner, who's a hairdresser renting a chair in a salon on the high street. I'm on the low side of pay at Marlow, and there aren't many other fit-out firms around here. I bought a used van and a set of tools for my weekend work last spring, so savings are under a month. My dad was a self-employed plumber, and I always wanted my own firm like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Bit of a let-down, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, nothing more, and people who got carried away should calm down. At work I'd keep showing the lads how I price jobs with it. Online I'd post a few short videos of my weekend jobs, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me fine. AI saves me hours on quotes, so I can do more weekend jobs and build my own name. The real worry is the van loan and restaurants closing when people tighten their belts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for pricing and certificates, and push the weekend work to two jobs every Saturday. I'd pay the van off faster, an extra fifty a month. And I'd go to the trade nights at the wholesaler to pick up contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty positive, with the usual money nerves. Nothing here stops me building what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by restaurants closing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three of the restaurants we fitted out in the last two years have already shut. When people stop eating out, Marlow gets fewer jobs, and I'm not senior enough to be safe. That's why the weekend work matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Sofia feel about you working weekends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's patient, but she wants Sundays. That's the deal: Saturdays for work, Sundays for her and Mass with my mum. Break that and I'm in trouble.

I'd keep posting **short videos** of my weekend jobs online.

The real worries are the **van loan** and restaurants closing.

Attend **trade nights** at the wholesaler for contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, booking, answering customers. That's my whole weekend admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work, and I'd mean it. At work I'd tell the lads to learn the tools now. Online I'd share how I run my weekend jobs with almost no admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. If AI does the booking and the quoting, a one-man firm can look like a five-man firm. The bit I'd watch is Marlow, because if their office staff get cut, the managers will push more on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI receptionist for the weekend work, taking calls and booking jobs. I'd register as a proper limited company within the year. And I'd stay at Marlow for the steady wage until the weekend work covers half the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a bit nervous. It feels like the door's opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people willing to work. What about the people this hurts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel for them, honestly. But I'd rather see them helped into a trade than paid to stay home. My cousin lost an admin job and now she's a plumber's mate, and she's happier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave Marlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the weekend work pays half the rent for six months straight. Not before. My dad always said never quit the steady job until the other one can feed you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years to AGI, robots by 2031. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to adapt fast and stop waiting for someone to save them. At work I'd be the one with a plan. I'd tell my mum not to worry, though she would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job is done in 2028, but I was already handing that to AI. What scares me is 2031, when a robot can fit kitchen lighting. I'd have three years to build a firm that owns robots instead of competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Marlow within a year and go full time on my own, using AI for everything except the tools in my hands. I'd save every penny for a robot lease when they appear. And I'd bring in a young apprentice, because I'd want someone with me when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, really nervous, but not frozen. I'd rather be scared and moving than scared and waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't leaving Marlow risky with so little saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. But in this version, staying is risky too. If Marlow's going to replace us with robots in 2031, I'd rather have three years building my own thing than three years waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sofia about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it'll be tight for a year, maybe two. She'd ask whether we can still afford the salon chair, and I'd say yes, because her income is our floor. People will still want a person cutting their hair for a while.

I'd reassure my **mum**, though she'd still worry.
think: The **thinking side** goes in 2028, but I was already handing it to AI.
By 2031 I need a firm that **owns robots**, not one competing with them.

fieldNote: He treats the **three-year gap** as a runway to build a firm.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is perfect for me. I build the firm properly, get a couple of regular restaurant clients and an apprentice. By 2034 I'm a small firm ready to buy a robot, not a worker scared of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time on my own in about two years, once the weekend work covers half the rent. I'd use AI for all the admin and pricing from day one. I'd take an apprentice in year three and look at a robot lease when the first ones are proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, a bit uneasy. The money's still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone who turns up on time and asks questions, like I did. I'd go through the parish youth group and the college. My dad took me on at fifteen, and I'd want to do that for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restaurants keep closing, or a big firm brings robots in early and undercuts everyone. Or I get injured and there's no income. I'd get proper insurance before I quit Marlow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. At work I'd say don't waste it. I'd tell my mum that by then I'll have my own firm, like Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is my best version. Ten years to build a firm, get known, train a couple of apprentices and save for robots. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine and the owner, not the worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Marlow three more years and build the weekend side slowly. I'd do the master electrician licence so I can sign off a firm's work. And Sofia and I would get married and maybe buy a small place before I go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Hopeful. This one feels like it was made for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this version worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual: money, health, restaurants. AI's not the scary bit here. Being poor at thirty is scarier than robots at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own firm to be known for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Turning up when we say and leaving it tidy. That's what my dad was known for. Robots or no robots, people remember that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years isn't long enough to build a firm on almost no savings. What would help is cheap business loans for tradespeople starting small firms, and apprenticeship funding so I could take a young person on without going under.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people who want to own something. Everyone talks about workers losing jobs, but a lot of us want to be the ones running the firm, robots included.

headlineQuote: A lot of us want to be the ones running the firm, robots included.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old electrician** at a fit-out firm doing restaurants, gyms and shops.
He runs **weekend jobs** with his own van and uses AI every day for pricing and certificates.
He lives with his partner, a hairdresser, with **under a month** saved after buying the van.
His goal is **his own firm**, like his plumber father, and he sees robots as tools to own.
He moves from **anxious to calm** as warning time grows, relying on self-reliance and planning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years is too short to build a firm on almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **business loans** for tradespeople starting small firms.
**Apprenticeship funding** so small firms can take young people on.
